brief.head: Credentials not needed
brief.text: When Amit Varma says hire the best, Ajay Shah said, he does not mean IIT or IIM badges but knowledge, character and connection with the world. {103-C12}

brief.head: Dream big, hire well
brief.text: Firms that position themselves as narrow bean counters get average employees, Ajay Shah said. Those chasing big audacious dreams are more likely to attract remarkable people. {103-C06}

brief.head: Who sets strategy?
brief.text: In India, Ajay Shah said, strategy tends to rest with a family promoter or a CEO. The institution of the board is only barely understood. {#boards}

brief.head: From cause to racket
brief.text: Ajay Shah offered a one-liner with “absolutely nothing to do with this episode”: every great idea starts out as a cause, then becomes a movement, then a racket. {103-J04}

brief.head: The glory of big firms
brief.text: The top 20,000 non-financial firms are pretty much the Indian economy, Ajay Shah said. “All the glory of modern capitalism is actually in the large companies.” {103-C09}

thought.text: Winning an argument is not as important as preserving the relationship.
thought.who: Brian Chesky’s line, which Amit Varma calls a key to his partnership with Ajay Shah

lead.kicker: Amit Varma’s thirteen rules for starting a business
lead.head: Mind your own business
body: The last episode ended with a bias for action. This one picked up there, with Amit Varma laying out thirteen more pieces of advice for anyone who might start a business, and Ajay Shah adding his own.
Even if you expect to be a banker all your life, Shah said, there is merit in kicking yourself and thinking: let’s start a business. Building one, he argued, makes you a better employee too.
Much of Varma’s advice came from clips of founders and investors such as Jeff Bezos, Sam Altman, Jensen Huang and Naval Ravikant.
## From project to company
Start as a specialist, Varma said, but become a generalist once the project becomes a company. {103-C01}

Then think from first principles. Elon Musk, he said, priced a battery from its raw materials and cut its cost from $600 to $80 per kilowatt hour, while experts said batteries could not be any cheaper.
“All progress happens because someone challenged the conventional thinking and on some margin the conventional thinking was wrong,” Varma said. {103-C03}

Then the customer, who is never to be blamed for a product’s failings. Then the product itself. Varma, who says he does 100 per cent product and 0 per cent marketing, quoted Kevin Hale: “Marketing is a tax you pay for not making your product awesome.”
Then a mission bigger than yourself, and a long horizon. “A long term commitment is the only arbitrage opportunity left in the market,” he said, quoting Altman.
## The people and the work
Choose co-founders above all for integrity, Varma said, and employees for values first, aptitude second and skill third.

Hard work, he said, is non-negotiable. Mandated 70-hour weeks are wrong, but voluntarily he could give every hour of his week when he is not sleeping. Burnout, he thinks, comes from worrying, procrastinating and overthinking, not from work.
And firms must build a culture of truth-telling, because humans did not evolve for it. “We’ve evolved to get along with each other,” Varma said. “We’ve not evolved to tell the truth.” {103-C14}
Shah tied this to what he called the central crisis of firms: in large, imperial companies, knowledge about customers and production does not bubble up to the top.
## Simple, proud and true

The last rules were about values. Simplicity first: Robinhood’s one screen, one button, one action, and Stripe’s five-minute integration. “The evolution to greatness is always an evolution towards simplicity,” Varma said. {103-C16}

Then professional pride, in work that nobody else will see. And finally Warren Buffett’s inner scorecard: his father’s lesson that you judge yourself by your own values, not by money, success or what people write about you.
“If you don’t score high on your inner scorecard, nothing is worth it,” Varma said. {103-C18}
Shah’s recommendation flowed from that: Clayton Christensen’s *How Will You Measure Your Life?*, “a beautiful, simple book”.

Varma, a literature student, said his twenty-year-old self would have been surprised by his conclusion: that some of our finest thinkers, among them Paul Graham and Naval Ravikant, are from the world of business.
He closed by urging viewers to share the episodes, like and subscribe, then caught himself. “Did I just say I will never do marketing? I will never do marketing, don’t bother.”

second.label: Never blame the user
second.head: University challenge
second.deck: Larry Page’s demo to Excite, and the lesson Aravind Srinivas drew from it
body: In the late 1990s, Amit Varma recalled, the search engines included Yahoo, Excite and Ask Jeeves. {103-J07} Larry Page took his PageRank technology to Excite to sell it. His engine, asked for “university”, found Harvard and Stanford; Excite found random junk.

Nobody types “university”, the Excite executive objected; a proper user would ask for the best Ivy League university in America. Page’s answer, in Varma’s telling: “You’re gaslighting the user. You’re saying the user is stupid.” {103-S02}

Aravind Srinivas of Perplexity, who tells the story, learnt from it. When his mother complained about her results, he nearly told her to fix the grammar of her question, then stopped himself: the fault was his, not hers.

quote.text: The problem is not with the user, the problem is with you.

second.caption: Larry Page’s demo to Excite

third.head: Gates tunes out the radio
body: Mike Moritz was being driven to the airport by Bill Gates, probably in the early 1980s, Amit Varma guessed. Where the car radio should have been, there was an empty slot. {103-R25}
Had someone stolen it? “No, no, no, no one stole it, I took it out,” Gates said. “Because if I listen to the radio, that’ll take away my time for thinking about Microsoft.” {103-S04}

Varma paired it with Jensen Huang, who does not wear a watch because “now is the most important time”. Obsession, in Apoorva Mehta’s definition, means the company is the last thing on your mind at night and the first in the morning.
Hard work is non-negotiable, Varma argued. A mandated 70-hour week is wrong; a chosen one is fine. “The path to excellence always comes with hard work.” {103-C13}
third.caption: Bill Gates’s missing car radio

p2.title: The founder’s rulebook
p2.deck: Amit Varma’s advice for anyone starting a business, argued over chapter by chapter with Ajay Shah

sections.label: The first rule
sections.head: What do they know of X?
sections.caption: being a generalist
body: Start as a specialist, and become a generalist the day your project turns into a company. That was Amit Varma’s first piece of advice, taken from a video by Sam Altman. {103-R02}

Larry Page and Sergey Brin were specialists while PageRank was a project, he said. A founder must step back and look at the world. Varma reached for Rudyard Kipling and C.L.R. James: what do they know of cricket who only cricket knows? {103-C01}
Ajay Shah noted that Google’s early slogan was not to be the best search engine but to organise the world’s information, an ambition that opened it to all kinds of adjacencies.

He warned that venture capitalists often keep founders to their last pitch deck. Varma recalled Vinod Khosla’s claim that seventy per cent of venture capitalists add negative value. {#negative} The burden of learning falls on the founder.
## Strategy is upside down

Shah then turned to the employee. The most important thinking in any firm, he said, is strategy: who are we, what are our capabilities, what amazing things can we do that the world will like? Marching orders flow from that down to the divisions.
An employee is told to shut up, be narrow and execute, Shah said. At the leadership level, it is upside down. {103-C02}
~ A leader must keep wondering, re-evaluating and changing his mind. That is why, he argued, thinking like a founder makes even a banker a better employee.

quote.text: So when you’re an employee, you’re being told to shut up, be narrow, execute, execute, execute. But at the leadership level, it’s upside down.

sections.label: The third rule
sections.head: Small is a luxury
sections.caption: acting small
body: In the last episode, Amit Varma urged founders to be inward-driven. Once the business exists, he said, the customer matters most, and the danger is noticing competitors more than customers.

Jeff Bezos, he said, decided very early on to focus on customers and not competitors. {#customers} He also preferred to ask what would stay the same: ten or twenty years on, people will still want lower prices, better value and faster delivery.

Above all, never blame the user. Founders get carried away by the Kool-Aid of their own product, Varma said, and dismiss the critic who doesn’t get it. He cast Ajay Shah as that critic, and Shah supplied the jab himself: “He’s a Unix command line user.” {103-J06}
## When small, act small
Garry Tan’s advice, Varma said, is that small companies should not mimic the polish of big ones, with a front page like Microsoft’s. Act small, and get close to the customer.
In the startup he ran before Y Combinator, Tan and his team answered customer emails personally. One day of the week, it was the CEO’s duty to answer every complaint himself. {#tanemails}
~ When you have a hundred or two hundred customers, Varma said, you can speak to every one of them. When you grow bigger, you can’t.

quote.text: smallness is a luxury that allows you to get that intimacy with your customer and build an incredible product.

sections.label: The fourth rule
sections.head: The tax on a dull product
sections.caption: product over marketing
body: Amit Varma’s fourth rule is close to his heart: don’t obsess over marketing. He quoted Kevin Hale of Y Combinator: “Marketing is a tax you pay for not making your product awesome.” {103-C05}

When people ask why he doesn’t cut clips of his shows for YouTube or Instagram, his answer has been that a good product is the best marketing. He built *The Seen and the Unseen* that way, he said, and thinks he has been proved right.

He does 100 per cent product and 0 per cent marketing. There may be an optimum, he conceded: with 5 or 10 per cent marketing, more of his tribe might find him. {#optimum} But he will not spend his limited bandwidth finding it.
## The danger in the mindset

Marketing is not bad, Varma said. The danger is that a marketing orientation takes over your thinking, pulling you towards the lowest common denominator and short-term gratification instead of building something great for the long term.
The same goes for people. Naval Ravikant calls networking overrated: do something great and your network will emerge. {103-R08}

~ Varma found the same. The wonderful people he has come to know came through his podcasts, not conferences or trade fairs. First make it awesome, he tells would-be founders, and everything will work out.

quote.text: Your tribe will eventually find you.

sections.label: The sixth rule
sections.head: A plan worth tearing up
sections.caption: thinking long-term
body: “A long term commitment is the only arbitrage opportunity left in the market,” Amit Varma said, quoting Sam Altman. {103-C07} Most people think about the next quarter; the long view is your edge.

Jeff Bezos wrote a 30-page business plan for Amazon knowing, as the VCs did, that it would fall apart on contact with reality. Everyone has a plan until they get punched in the face, as Ajay Shah put it, supplying Mike Tyson’s line. “But that exercise of writing thirty pages is important,” Varma said, “because it clarifies your thinking.” {103-S08}

Vinod Khosla’s rule is to be obstinate about your vision and flexible about your tactics. Eric Schmidt even recommends five-year plans. The hosts are no fans of those for India’s economy, Varma said, because an economy can’t be centrally planned; a company can. {103-J10}
## Rethink HR

Shah has met many senior managers who preach long-term thinking while HR pays bonuses on narrow targets over a quarter or a year. Then why would anyone take more risks? If your people are short-sighted, he said, it is your fault. {103-C08}

~ His fix is to speak in compounding numbers that excite people: 5x in five years, 10x in ten. A 14 per cent nominal growth a year for five years is a doubling. {#doubling} That pushes managers to lay the foundations of a bigger firm.

quote.text: The bane of India is short term thinking.

sections.label: The seventh rule
sections.head: Teach your founders well
sections.caption: choosing a co-founder
body: Amit Varma asked Ajay Shah for his favourite Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young song, fishing for *Teach Your Children*. Shah offered *Helpless* and *Southern Cross*. “See, we don’t script anything,” Varma said, and moved on: choose your founders well. {103-J11}
Patrick Collison, he said, thinks starting with someone you are close to is a feature, not a bug. Brian Chesky’s reason: you will spend more time with your co-founder than with your spouse. {103-R19}
Ten or fifteen years ago, with his male macho ego, Varma would have thought winning an argument was everything. Today what matters to him is the relationship.

Naval Ravikant looks for high intelligence, high energy and high integrity, and of those, by far the most important is integrity. {#integrity} Garry Tan warns against co-CEOs, because every decision below them slows down.
## Arguing to learn

Shah added that a great partnership brings different knowledge to the table, and both partners do Bayesian updating. It hardly matters which decision is taken, because both come out stronger. The point, he said, is to jointly build a theory of the world and of the firm. {103-C11}
~ People too sure of themselves to update, Shah said, have a serious character defect.

quote.text: And the purpose of the disagreement actually is to build a model of the world.

sections.label: The tenth rule
sections.head: Clubbed for the truth
sections.caption: optimising for truth-telling
body: Jeff Bezos’s advice, which Amit Varma made his own, is to optimise for truth-telling. Humans are social animals, Varma said. A truth-teller could be clubbed to death in a tribe. {103-C14}

So organisations drift, by default, towards deference up the hierarchy and politeness among peers. Firms must build mechanisms and a culture against this. One is Bezos’s practice of disagree and commit, from his interview with Lex Fridman: argue, then fully own the decision, with no “I told you so” later. {103-R34}
## The imperial firm

Ajay Shah called information the central crisis of firms. Knowledge about customers in each locale, and the best way to produce there, exists inside the firm. In large, imperial firms it does not bubble up. {103-C15}
Often, he said, a top team is “thrilled to bits” at its own success and sure it has the one right answer for the whole world. It pushes orders down and stops listening, and productivity suffers.

~ Varma added that big companies often fail this way. Kodak had digital photography within the company and did nothing with it. {#kodak} Incentives and silos played a part, he said, but so did truth failing to travel upward.

quote.text: We’ve evolved to get along with each other. Right? We’ve not evolved to tell the truth.

side.boxText: Jeff Bezos turns up more than anyone in Amit Varma’s advice, which came mostly from short clips of founders and investors. Many were found on Startup Archive, an Instagram account Varma follows. {103-R41}

contQuote.text: When you build a successful business, the only way it can be successful is by providing value to people, by making individuals better off, and eventually at scale making society better off.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A plane meal, one room, a lamp post and a lion

stories.start: I will often do this thing where I will go on YouTube
stories.end: is to actually lie about it and say take care
stories.caption: Nonstop Dan’s missing meal
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on an airline crew that would not own up
stories.head: The vegan meal that wasn’t
body: Amit Varma likes watching YouTube videos of luxury resorts and of business and first class on flights. A reviewer he trusts is Nonstop Dan, who flies business class all year, pays for it himself and makes videos of it.
The two times Varma has flown business class abroad, he chose the airline from Dan’s videos, and got exactly the experience Dan described, pros and cons included.
Two days before the recording, Dan posted a video on Air India. Its new business class, he said, was absolutely awesome: higher walls, more privacy, a door you can close.

Then came the food. Dan had ordered a special meal, a vegan one, Varma thinks, and it had not been loaded. The crew served him a dish and insisted it was his vegan meal. He read the ingredients, found cheese, and pointed out that it was the regular dish on the menu.
He kept arguing. A superior was called, and seemed just as lost. At the second meal, the same thing happened.

Dan was furious, and Varma thought rightly so. In Varma’s telling, Dan asked: “What if I had a food allergy? What if I said I’m allergic to peanuts and there were peanuts in something? And not only did these people not know it, they lied to me about it.” {103-S06}

~ The right answer, Varma said, was simple: apologise, admit the meal had been forgotten, offer what was on board in economy and first class, and make it up to him after the flight with a refund or points.
stories.why: A culture of truth-telling has to be built, Varma argued, because humans evolved to get along. The reflex to cover up is the one that makes people on the street confidently give directions they don’t know. {103-J19}
stories.postscript: Varma allows one exception. If your lady love asks whether she looks fat in a dress, “there is only one answer”. {103-J20}

stories.start: There's this wonderful uh friend Ajay Korshall of Build Desk
stories.end: glory in the picture, and that's precisely the kind of culture
stories.caption: BillDesk’s three founders
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a firm run by three founders in one room
stories.head: Three’s company at BillDesk
body: Garry Tan, Amit Varma said, warns against co-CEOs, because two people must sign off on every decision. Ajay Shah had a story that cuts the other way.

His friend Ajay Kaushal co-founded BillDesk, a very successful Indian firm. Its big exit was snarled up by Indian government delays; but for that, Shah said, it would have been one of the biggest exits in Indian history.

Its three co-founders sit in one room and argue over every important decision, and none wants to be sole CEO. “So they think none of us is good enough to do it alone,” Shah said. They worked that way with no employees and still do with ten thousand. {103-S05}
~ Shah credits Kaushal’s character: quiet, unassuming and humble, interested in the idea and the argument, never in flaunting his own glory. “Ajays are awesome,” Varma said. {103-J12}
stories.why: Varma called it an outlier, but a lesson all the same: a single CEO is not a hard and fast rule. Think for yourself, he said, from your values and your own circumstances, rather than getting into a groove.

stories.start: I love the story that Simon Sinek tells about Nike and Phil Knight
stories.end: something to do with your personality, your dreams, and who you are
stories.caption: the guy under the lamp post
stories.kicker: Amit Varma retells Simon Sinek’s story of Phil Knight
stories.head: Just do it, in the dark
body: At a conference, Simon Sinek recalls, Phil Knight of Nike asked everyone who ran for exercise to stand. Most of the room stood up. {103-R11}

Then he thinned them out, first those who ran less than once a week, then less than twice. Only those who ran at least three times a week, rain or shine, feeling good or bad, stayed standing: a handful.

The next time you are out before dawn, Knight told them, “running in the darkness and it’s wet and you’re feeling miserable and you’re still running”, and there is a guy under the lamp post cheering you on, “that’s us”. {103-S03}
~ Amit Varma said the story moves him. With a brand like that, the story is no longer about selling cool sneakers but about your personality, your dreams and who you are.

quote.text: Just do it is not about winning. It is about doing.

stories.start: There's something that Nawal Ravikant again says which uh ties in with stuff
stories.end: make the important and not urgent into important but urgent, like calendarizing them
stories.caption: working like a lion
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on why he works in bursts
stories.head: Sleep, sprint, repeat
body: Amit Varma has long lamented that, in Eisenhower’s matrix, he lives in two quadrants: not important and not urgent, or important and urgent, as when an episode must be shot. Tim Urban, he said, wrote about the same dilemma. {103-R32}
Then came Naval Ravikant’s advice: work like a lion. A lion sleeps eighteen hours and chills most of the time, then puts in a furious sprint. {#lion}

Humans were shaped in the hunter-gatherer age, Varma reasoned, and focusing hard burns calories. “So it is natural for us, it is efficient for us, it is rational for us to get distracted because we save the calories for the hunt.” {103-S10}
~ There is no right or wrong about it, he said. His fix: accept the wiring, and use hacks such as calendarising to make the important urgent.
stories.why: Seeing a flaw as evolved wiring removes the shame and points to workarounds. The hosts teach the same in their course *Life Lessons*: amplify what is good in our wiring and mitigate what is bad.

quiz.q: What did Bill Gates tell Mike Moritz had happened to the radio in his car?
quiz.a: He took it out himself, so he could think about Microsoft.

quiz.q: Which word did Larry Page search for to show Excite what PageRank could do?
quiz.a: “University”: his engine found Harvard and Stanford, while Excite returned random junk.

quiz.q: How long did it take to integrate PayPal into a website, and how long Stripe?
quiz.a: About seven days, with a hundred-page manual; Stripe took five minutes.

quiz.q: At Phil Knight’s talk, who is the guy under the lamp post cheering runners on?
quiz.a: Nike: the brand that is with you when you do, not only when you win.

quiz.q: What did Warren Buffett’s father teach him to be guided by?
quiz.a: His inner scorecard of values, not the outer one of money and reputation.

quiz.q: According to Sam Altman, what is the only arbitrage opportunity left in the market?
quiz.a: A long-term commitment, when everyone else is chasing the next quarter.
